observation: Running large language model (LLM) inference over large relational datasets for batch data analytics is extremely slow and expensive: an NVIDIA L4 GPU serving Llama3-8B processes only about 6 KB of text per second, taking roughly a day to handle 15 GB of data, and processing a comparable amount of data on OpenAI's GPT-4o costs about $10K. Although LLM invocations are increasingly offered as operators on relational tables, naively sending rows in their default order to a serving backend with a prompt KV cache leads to low cache-hit rates. Real relational workloads contain repeated cell values, joined-feature repetition, popular-item reuse, and shared RAG contexts that could serve as cached prefixes; but tables also contain highly unique leading fields such as IDs or review text, and the fixed row/field order in which requests are sent critically limits how much prefix reuse is possible.

claims: Serving systems for large language models reuse the cached attention key/value states of prompt prefixes to avoid recomputing prompt processing for repeated requests.
PagedAttention and RadixAttention provide the memory-management and cache-lookup primitives that make prefix sharing practical in general-purpose LLM serving systems.
Because key/value reuse is triggered by exact token prefixes, whether two requests can share computation is determined by the textual order in which their prompts are assembled.

works.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs

claims: Prompt Cache generalizes prefix caches by allowing an arbitrary prompt to be decomposed into application-level modules whose attention states have already been cached.

Even modular caching assumes that reusable text appears exactly as a previously cached module, so it still depends on how a relational row's values are concatenated and on which values are placed together.

works.title: Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency Inference

claims: A recent line of systems embeds LLM calls into SQL/dataframe query processors, making them relational-style operators over whole tables.

LOTUS provides semantic operators such as filtering, joining, and aggregating by prompting an LLM for every relevant tuple or group, while TableGPT and DB-GPT couple LLM reasoning with tables and databases.
These systems focus on operator semantics and output quality and do not consider reordering the rows or columns of the issued prompts to maximize KV-cache reuse.

works.title: LOTUS: Enabling Semantic Queries with Large Language Models
TableGPT: Towards Unifying Tables with Large Language Models
DB-GPT: Large Language Model Meets Database

claims: Approaches that feed relational data to LLMs generally serialize each record by concatenating feature names and cell values in the order the columns appear in the input schema or dataframe.
This serialization work optimizes the text representation for semantic accuracy of a few-shot classifier or a data-understanding agent, rather than for prefix reuse in an inference backend.

works.title: TabLLM: Few-Shot Classification of Tabular Data with Large Language Models
